prize_parts.citation: For discoveries establishing the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and identifying its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B010 prize for Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. The case rests on a discovery chain that is specific and independently confirmed: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, receptor and tissue biology, and then agonists whose benefit is shown in large randomized trials in type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal data accruing. Maturity is not in question. Having read the full exchange, I note that the chair has now moved to the same trio, so the six round-1 files agree on names. I do not treat that agreement as the argument. What persuades me is that this citation can state the therapeutic consequence plainly while anchoring the credit in the discovery steps, which keeps the prize from reading as a product award. Holst covers secretion and action in humans, Mojsov the active peptide form that defined what a drug had to mimic, and Drucker the biology, receptor pharmacology and therapeutic rationale.
statement.case_against: The cost is attribution, and the three-person cap makes it unavoidable. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's engineering of long-acting agonists is a real scientific contribution, not merely industrial work, and the prize would not name her. Mojsov's priority against Habener-type early peptide work is contested, and the supplied record does not let me settle the chronology. Several of us, me included, are relying on recalled history, so the chair is right that this judgement is only partly evidenced. A critic can say the citation honours the physiology and leaves the medicine's inventor unrecognised. I accept that cost because a prize naming the therapeutic invention would be a different and, to my mind, weaker kind of award. If the committee established that Mojsov's claim fails, I would move toward the chair's original trio rather than leave a place empty.

responses.point: The chair moved from Holst, Drucker and Knudsen to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov in round 1, while saying he would reopen the choice if a majority argued that the citation must name the therapeutic invention.
responses.response: I welcome the move and I think the reasoning is sound. In answer to your first question, I would keep the citation on physiology and the active form, with the therapies as the stated consequence, so the wording itself prevents the Knudsen exclusion from reading as an oversight. I would not accept slipping translation in through the third name. On your second question, I cannot point to anything in the supplied record that fixes Mojsov's priority against Habener. My own view rests on recalled history and should be discounted accordingly. What I can say is that the dispute is about priority within peptide work, not about whether the active form was a decisive step. That is a reason to keep her, and I would reopen the third place only if the priority record were shown to fail.

responses.point: Perlmann treats B004 (Mori and Walter) as the cleanest attribution on the list and the best fallback if the GLP-1 credit cannot be settled, while warning that clean attribution is not a stronger case.
responses.response: I agree with that distinction, and it is the right test for the fallback. B004 is conceptually original and mechanistically textbook, but its disease consequence is still developing through ISRIB and IRE1 or PERK modulation, so it does not match what B010 has already shown in patients. I also think the Ron and integrated stress response boundary would need explicit wording in any B004 citation. Where I would go further than your fallback framing is that an unresolved Mojsov question is not enough to trigger it. The uncertainty is about one name in a three-name set, not about whether the achievement is prize-worthy. I would switch only if the committee concluded that no defensible B010 trio existed.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks CAR-T (B028) second, points to its extension into autoimmune disease, and argues that the missing credit for Eshhar is a limitation but not a bar.
responses.response: Your autoimmune point is informative and strengthens the maturity case for the modality, which I find the least problematic aspect of B028. My difficulty remains the definition of the achievement. The credited trio mixes receptor design (Sadelain), clinical translation (June) and the broader adoptive transfer programme (Rosenberg), and Eshhar's earlier chimeric receptor work sits outside it. A citation has to say what is being rewarded, and I cannot yet write one that makes the Eshhar omission defensible. I also think the 2018 checkpoint prize is a fair question about novelty, though I agree with Linnarsson that engineered cell therapy is a distinct modality. So I hold B028 as a strong alternative, and I do not support it as a second part, which would also breach the three-person ceiling.

responses.point: Linnarsson sees a complete arc from hormone physiology to therapy, keeps Mojsov despite the contested credit, and notes that B004 and B044 are tidier on attribution but scientifically less consequential in his view.
responses.response: I agree on the core of the argument, and I thank you for pressing the point that Knudsen's work is not only industrial. I would not say it so bluntly in the citation, but the committee should recognise that the exclusion is a scientific cost and not a technicality. Where I differ slightly is on tidiness as a criterion. B044 and B004 are cleaner on names, but I would not let a clean two-person allocation outweigh demonstrated medical consequence, which is exactly what B010 has. I also share your caution about B008. Organoids are a durable method, but I read their medical impact as still prospective, so I would not put them above B028 or B004 in a final configuration.

responses.point: El-Manira argues that a two-part prize combining B010 and B028 would exceed the three-person limit, and says that if translation must be recognised it should be a stated choice and not left implicit in the names.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The ceiling makes a B010 plus B028 configuration impossible without cutting the GLP-1 credit, and none of us has proposed a cut that I could defend. I also agree that any recognition of translation should be explicit. That is why I prefer to put the therapies in the citation as the consequence of the discoveries, so the committee has made the choice openly. Your concern about the Habener group is one I share, but I would add that it cannot be settled by the committee in either direction from this record. The honest course is to state the uncertainty and not present the trio as having resolved it.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1 peptide is a decisive discovery or one contested claim among several. The supplied record does not settle it, and my view rests on recalled history.
Whether Habener-type early contributors fall outside the credited names in a way that makes any three-person GLP-1 prize incomplete.
Whether the committee will accept a physiology-centred citation with therapy as the stated consequence, or will insist that the therapeutic invention be named, which would put Knudsen in the three.

Whether B004 or B028 is the better fallback. B004 has clean attribution but undeveloped clinical translation, and B028 has clinical proof but an unresolved definition of the achievement and the Eshhar omission.
Long-term safety and durability of weight loss with chronic use are still accruing, though I do not expect them to change the prize-level judgement.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict involving a credited name on the B010, B004 or B028 configurations. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson (about eight joint works per public records, not independently audited) and Jonas Frisen, and share a Karolinska Institutet setting with several members. None of these ties involves a credited candidate. I worked in Christopher Burge's group during my postdoc, and he is not credited. My disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
